title: Apple Watch case: production study
summary: Reverse-engineered an aluminium smartwatch case and designed the machining line to make one million of them a year — process plan, tooling, capacity and cost.
role: Team of 2 · CAD, process plan, capacity & cost

cover.alt: Dimensioned manufacturing drawing of the watch case

tldr: Rebuilt the case geometry from public drawings and teardown photos; assigned functional tolerances.
Planned the route from 10 mm Al 7005-T6 sheet to a finished part: laser blanking, cavity and external milling, vibratory finishing.
Sized the line for 1M parts/year and resolved a milling bottleneck by scheduling the fleet over four periods.
facts: Geometry, drawings, process plan, capacity and cost model (with Alessia Aguzzi)

sections.title: Geometry and tolerances
body: Only the external surfaces are public, so we inferred the internals — battery cavity, crown and button seats, microphone and strap slots — from teardown photos, then assigned tolerances by function: ±0.01 mm on precision fits, ±0.1 mm on structural walls, and a Ø0.05 mm concentricity on the Ø3 H7 crown bore.

sections.title: Process route
body: Seven steps from raw sheet to finished case. Use the arrows to go through them.

items.alt: Drawing of the 1500 by 1000 mm panel with the grid of 608 blanks and the locating-hole detail
items.title: Sheet to panels
items.text: A 3000 × 1500 × 10 mm Al 7005-T6 sheet is laser-cut (AMADA REGIUS fibre laser) into three 1500 × 1000 mm panels. Each panel holds 608 blanks; Ø6 H7 holes locate it on the machine.

items.alt: CAD of the internal cavity milled into the blank, with dimensions
items.title: Cavities milled on the panel
items.text: After facing, the internal cavity of every blank is milled from both sides while the blanks are still joined — the panel itself holds them.

items.title: Blank separation
items.text: The 608 blanks are cut out of the panel, each one already carrying its internal geometry.

items.alt: Drawing of the microphone hole with detail views
items.title: Small features
items.text: Microphone hole, button and crown seats: features small enough to need 1 mm tools, which is why the DATRON MLCube's 60,000 rpm spindle was chosen.

items.alt: CAD and drawing of the external wall machining
items.title: External surfaces
items.text: External walls and strap attachments are machined on the single part, holding ±0.01 mm on the critical outer dimensions.

items.title: Finishing
items.text: Vibratory tumbling with low-aggressiveness plastic cones brings the surface from Ra 0.8 to the Ra 0.4 µm target without rounding the edges (30-minute cycle).

items.alt: Chart of how the 89 CNC centres are split between cavity milling and external machining across four periods
items.title: Sizing the line
items.text: 1,000,000 parts a year needs 1 laser cutter, 89 CNC centres and 1 tumbler. Cavity milling is the bottleneck, so the fleet is reassigned between phases over four periods instead of buying more machines.

sections.title: Capacity, tooling and cost
body: For every operation we computed removed volume, material-removal rate and cutting power, and from those the machining time and energy. Tool life came from Taylor's law (literature values for carbide on aluminium, n = 0.25, C = 900 m/min), which set how many parts each tool makes before it's changed. A cost model rolls machine amortisation, maintenance, energy and tooling into a cost per part.

body.note: An academic study of a public product, not work for Apple: internal geometry, tolerances, machine prices and tool-life constants are our assumptions and were not validated with machining trials.
